In this lab, you will build your own nonstationary model of extreme daily rainfall at Houston Hobby Airport and decide whether the evidence supports a published claim that it is rising.
Everyone uses the same record, and each of you makes different choices along the way.
On Wednesday, October 7, you will present your results in class and defend those choices, as practice for the oral exam.

## Objectives

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

1. Build a nonstationary extreme value model, choosing annual maxima or peaks over threshold, a covariate, and the form of the trend.
1. Report a change in the 100-year rainfall with an interval, and say what the interval leaves out.
1. Defend each choice behind your result.

## Setup

First, load the packages.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| output: false
using Pkg
here = dirname(@__FILE__)
Pkg.activate(here)
Pkg.instantiate()

using CEVE543Utils
using CairoMakie, CSV, DataFrames, Dates, Distributions, LaTeXStrings
using Printf, Random, Statistics
using FlexiChains: summarystats

rng = MersenneTwister(543)
set_theme!(theme_minimal(); fontsize=14)
colors = Makie.wong_colors()
```

### Rainfall data

You will analyze daily precipitation at Houston Hobby Airport, station `USW00012918` in NOAA's Global Historical Climatology Network, which is the record from Monday's lectures.
The file `hobby-daily.csv` has one row for each day with a valid reading, with the rainfall in the column `prcp_mm`, in millimeters.

@fig-daily plots every wet day.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-daily
#| fig-cap: "Daily rainfall at Houston Hobby Airport, wet days only."
daily = CSV.read(joinpath(here, "hobby-daily.csv"), DataFrame)
daily.year = year.(daily.date)
wet = filter(r -> r.prcp_mm > 0, daily)

fig = Figure(; size=(700, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{date}", ylabel=L"\text{daily rainfall (mm)}")
scatter!(ax, wet.date, wet.prcp_mm; color=colors[1], markersize=3)
fig
```

Not every year is complete.
@fig-days-per-year counts the days with a valid reading in each year.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-days-per-year
#| fig-cap: "Days with a valid reading in each year at Houston Hobby Airport."
days_per_year = combine(groupby(daily, :year), nrow => :n_days)
fig = Figure(; size=(700, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{year}", ylabel=L"\text{days with a valid reading}")
scatterlines!(ax, days_per_year.year, days_per_year.n_days; color=colors[1], markersize=5)
fig
```

Many years are missing days, and 2026 is not over yet, so you need to decide how to handle the gaps.
Assume the data are *missing at random*: whether a day was recorded has nothing to do with how much rain fell.
To see when this might fail, picture a rain gauge that breaks in the heaviest storms.
A simple approach is to keep only the years with at least some number of valid days, such as 350.
You are welcome to try other cutoffs or other ways to filter.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| output: false
keep = days_per_year.year[(days_per_year.n_days .>= 350) .& (days_per_year.year .<= 2025)]
filter!(r -> r.year in keep, daily)
```

### Covariates

You have three candidate covariates in `covariates.csv`, one row per year from 1880 to 2025:

| Column | What it is | Source |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `log_CO2` | Natural log of annual mean atmospheric CO2, in parts per million | Before 1959, the Law Dome ice core record [@etheridge_lawdomeco2:1996; @macfarlingmeure_lawdomeextended:2006]; from 1959, the Mauna Loa annual means from NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory |
| `gmst` | Global mean surface temperature anomaly, in °C relative to 1951-1980 | NASA's GISTEMP version 4, January to December mean |
| `nino34` | Sea surface temperature anomaly in the Niño 3.4 region of the tropical Pacific, in °C relative to 1981-2010 | HadISST, from NOAA's Physical Sciences Laboratory, mean of the 12 calendar months |

CO2 and global temperature both rise over the record, so they are candidates for a long-term trend.
Niño 3.4 measures the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, which shifts from year to year with no long-term trend, so it is a candidate for explaining which years are wet.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-covariates
#| fig-cap: "The three candidate covariates over the years of the Hobby record."
covariates = filter(r -> r.year >= 1930, CSV.read(joinpath(here, "covariates.csv"), DataFrame))
fig = Figure(; size=(700, 500))
for (k, (col, label)) in enumerate(((:log_CO2, "log CO2"), (:gmst, "GMST anomaly (°C)"), (:nino34, "Niño 3.4 anomaly (°C)")))
    lines!(Axis(fig[k, 1]; ylabel=label, xlabel=k == 3 ? "year" : ""), covariates.year, covariates[!, col]; color=colors[k])
end
fig
```

## Your challenge

@fagnant_spatiotemporal:2020 analyzed more than 600 rain gauges in southeast Texas and reported that the 100-year daily rainfall at Hobby rose by 1.93 mm per year (95% interval 1.50 to 2.35).
In this lab, you will analyze the same station, choose your own rule for which years to keep, and fit your own model.
Their rule for keeping years differs from yours, so your answer need not match theirs.
You will choose whether to fit a GEV to annual maxima or a GPD to peaks over threshold, which covariates to use and how each parameter depends on them, and which priors to include.

Prepare a 5-10 minute slide presentation for class on Wednesday, October 7, that leads with your results and then explains your modeling choices.
Upload your slides to the Canvas page for the Lab 6 presentations before class on Wednesday.
Answer these four key questions.

1. What is your best estimate for the 10- and 100-year return levels in 2026?
1. How uncertain are these estimates?
1. How have these return levels changed over the past 40 years?
1. How will these return levels change over the next 40 years, and what assumptions do you make in projecting these?

Explain each key decision below, saying what you chose and why.

1. Did you fit a GEV to annual maxima or a GPD to peaks over threshold?
   If you fit a GEV, how did you handle years with missing data?
   If you fit a GPD, how did you decluster, and how did you choose the threshold?
1. How did you decide between a stationary and a nonstationary model?
   If nonstationary, how did you choose the covariates and the functional form?
   If stationary, what gave you confidence in that choice?
1. How did you estimate your uncertainty?
   If you used a Bayesian fit, how did you choose the priors?
   If you used a bootstrap, how did you choose how to resample?

## Examples

You make more of the choices in this lab than in any earlier one.
Two worked examples on synthetic (simulated) data give you all the code you need.
Keep this section as a reference while you work; you may delete all of it, both the GEV and the GPD examples, from the notebook you turn in.

### GEV example

In the first example, you fit a GEV with a quadratic trend in the location and the log scale.
A quadratic is a poor choice for a real record, for the reasons under Other functional forms, but it uses every keyword you will need.

$$
y_t \sim \text{GEV}\left(\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 x_t + \alpha_2 x_t^2, \; \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + \beta_2 x_t^2), \; \xi\right).
$$

The covariate is the year centered on 1985, $x_t = t - 1985$.
The synthetic dataset has one annual maximum for each year from 1946 to 2025.
In 1985 its location rises by 0.5 mm per year and its scale shrinks by 0.5% per year; by 1990 both trends have reversed.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| output: false
years = collect(1946:2025)
x = years .- 1985
μ_true = 90 .+ 0.5 .* x .- 0.05 .* x .^ 2
σ_true = 35 .* exp.(-0.005 .* x .+ 0.0005 .* x .^ 2)
y_syn = rand.(rng, GeneralizedExtremeValue.(μ_true, σ_true, 0.15))
```

The `gevfitbayes` function from the `CEVE543Utils` package fits a GEV whose location and log scale are each a linear combination of the covariates you pass.
Passing $x_t$ and $x_t^2$ as two covariates gives the quadratic above:

```{julia}
#| solution: false
gev_syn = gevfitbayes(y_syn; locationcov=[x, x .^ 2], logscalecov=[x, x .^ 2], rng=rng, progress=false)
DataFrame(summarystats(gev_syn.estimate))
```

`locationcov` and `logscalecov` each take a list of covariates, so `[x, x .^ 2]` is two of them.
`rng` is the random number generator from the setup cell, and `progress=false` hides the progress bar.

By default, priors in `gevfitbayes` are flat on every coefficient and uniform between $-0.5$ and $0.5$ on $\xi$.
The posterior is sampled with DE-MCzs, the sampler in the RMC-BestFit software that @smith_brays:2026 use.
Pass `sampler=NUTS()` to use the NUTS sampler instead.

The `summarystats` table is for checking the chains.
Check the `rhat` column, which should be close to 1, and the `ess_bulk` column, which should be in the hundreds or more, as in lab 5.
DE-MCzs takes no gradient steps, so it has no divergences to count.
Before sampling, the fit centers each covariate and divides it by its standard deviation, so a slope in that table is a change per standard deviation of the covariate.

`params` gives the coefficients in the units of the covariate: a matrix for each of `β_location`, `β_logscale`, and `β_shape`, with one row per posterior draw and one column per coefficient.
The first column is the intercept, which is the value at the means of the covariates rather than at $x_t = 0$.
The second column is $\alpha_1$, the slope per year in 1985, and the third is $\alpha_2$.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
coefs = params(gev_syn)
α1 = coefs.β_location[:, 2]
@printf("α1: median %.2f mm per year [%.2f, %.2f]; the true value is 0.5\n",
    median(α1), quantile(α1, 0.025), quantile(α1, 0.975))
```

`returnlevel` computes return levels at any covariate value you pass, giving one row per posterior draw and one column per value.
Here the values are the years you want minus 1985, and their squares.
So `rl100[:, 1]` is the 100-year level in 1986, `rl100[:, 2]` in 2026, and `rl100[:, 3]` in 2066, with one entry per draw.
The cell also defines `interval`, which rounds the 2.5%, 50%, and 97.5% quantiles of the draws to whole millimeters: a 95% interval with the median in the middle.
Each `println` line reports the 100-year level; to report the 10-year level, use `rl10` in place of `rl100`.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
report_years = [1986, 2026, 2066]
x_report = report_years .- 1985
rl10 = returnlevel(gev_syn, 10; locationcov=[x_report, x_report .^ 2], logscalecov=[x_report, x_report .^ 2])
rl100 = returnlevel(gev_syn, 100; locationcov=[x_report, x_report .^ 2], logscalecov=[x_report, x_report .^ 2])

interval(v) = round.(quantile(v, [0.025, 0.5, 0.975]))
println("100-year level in 2026 (mm): ", interval(rl100[:, 2]))
println("Change, 1986 to 2026 (mm): ", interval(rl100[:, 2] .- rl100[:, 1]))
println("Change, 2026 to 2066 (mm): ", interval(rl100[:, 3] .- rl100[:, 2]))
```

The projection to 2066 assumes the quadratic keeps going for another 40 years, past the end of the data.
With log CO2 or GMST as the covariate, you also have to choose a value for that covariate in 2066, and say what it is and why.

@fig-syn-trend plots the fitted 2- and 100-year levels in each year of the record next to the true levels the synthetic data came from.
With no covariates passed, `returnlevel` evaluates at each year in the record.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-syn-trend
#| fig-cap: "The 2- and 100-year levels through time from the GEV fit to the synthetic record (posterior median), the true levels, and the synthetic annual maxima."
fig = Figure(; size=(700, 350))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{year}", ylabel=L"\text{daily rainfall (mm)}")

for (k, T) in enumerate([2, 100])
    rl_fit = returnlevel(gev_syn, T)
    rl_true = returnlevel.(GeneralizedExtremeValue.(μ_true, σ_true, 0.15), T)
    lines!(ax, years, median.(eachcol(rl_fit)); color=colors[k], linewidth=2, label="$T-year level, fitted")
    lines!(ax, years, rl_true; color=colors[k], linestyle=:dash, label="$T-year level, true")
end

scatter!(ax, years, y_syn; color=:black, markersize=5, label="synthetic annual maxima")
axislegend(ax; position=:lt)
fig
```

You can also fit by maximum likelihood and get an interval from a bootstrap.
`gevfit` fits the same model by maximum likelihood, and `getdistribution` gives the fitted GEV for each year.
A parametric bootstrap draws a new record from those distributions, refits it, and records its return levels, many times over.
The spread of the refitted levels is the uncertainty.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
gev_mle = gevfit(y_syn; locationcov=[x, x .^ 2], logscalecov=[x, x .^ 2])
gev_by_year = getdistribution(gev_mle)

n_boot = 500
rl100_boot = zeros(n_boot, length(report_years))
for b in 1:n_boot
    y_boot = rand.(rng, gev_by_year)
    fit_boot = gevfit(y_boot; locationcov=[x, x .^ 2], logscalecov=[x, x .^ 2])
    rl100_boot[b, :] = returnlevel(fit_boot, 100; locationcov=[x_report, x_report .^ 2], logscalecov=[x_report, x_report .^ 2])
end

println("100-year level in 2026 (mm): ", interval(rl100_boot[:, 2]))
println("Change, 1986 to 2026 (mm): ", interval(rl100_boot[:, 2] .- rl100_boot[:, 1]))
println("Change, 2026 to 2066 (mm): ", interval(rl100_boot[:, 3] .- rl100_boot[:, 2]))
```

### Other functional forms

You choose the functional form: which parameters change with the covariate, and how.
Every fitting function also takes a table and the names of its columns.
For example, `gevfitbayes(annmax, :y; locationcovid=[:log_CO2], logscalecovid=[:log_CO2])` fits the column `y` of the table `annmax`, with the location and the log scale each a line in `log_CO2`.
You build `annmax` under Your Hobby analysis below.
With this table form, each functional form is a choice of covariate columns:

- For a trend in the location alone, pass `locationcovid` and leave out `logscalecovid`.
- For a trend in the scale alone, pass `logscalecovid` and leave out `locationcovid`.
- Leave out both to fit a stationary model.
- For a curved trend, add a column holding the covariate squared to your table, such as `annmax.log_CO2_sq = annmax.log_CO2 .^ 2`, and name it in `locationcovid`.
  A quadratic will find some curvature in almost any record, including one drawn from a straight line.
  Outside the data it grows without limit, so its 2066 level depends on a curvature the record barely pins down.
- For an abrupt change at a year you choose, add a column that is 0 before that year and 1 after it.
  Say why that year, and whether you chose it before or after looking at the data.

### Prior information

You change the priors with two keywords.
`trend_priors` puts a prior on the slopes, one for each parameter, and any you leave out stay flat.
The slope priors are on the standardized scale of the `summarystats` table, so each is a change per standard deviation of the covariate.
A `location` slope is in millimeters, so `trend_priors=(location=Normal(0, 5),)` says the location probably moves less than about 10 mm per standard deviation.
The trailing comma makes it a named tuple with one entry.
A `logscale` slope is a proportional change in the scale, so `logscale=Normal(0, 0.1)` says the scale probably changes by less than about 20% per standard deviation.
`quantile_priors` states what you believe about return levels, as in lab 4.
Each belief gives the position of a year in the record (`index=1` is the first year), a return period, and a distribution for that return level in that year.
You can give as many as you like.
The two beliefs below are hypothetical, made up to suit the synthetic record.
For Hobby, base a belief on a source you can name, and say what it is.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
beliefs = [
    (index=1, period=100, belief=Normal(250, 40)),
    (index=lastindex(y_syn), period=100, belief=Normal(450, 40)),
]
gev_beliefs = gevfitbayes(y_syn; locationcov=[x, x .^ 2], logscalecov=[x, x .^ 2], quantile_priors=beliefs, rng=rng, progress=false)
rl100_beliefs = returnlevel(gev_beliefs, 100; locationcov=[x_report, x_report .^ 2], logscalecov=[x_report, x_report .^ 2])
@printf("2026 100-year level: median %.0f mm without beliefs, %.0f mm with them\n", median(rl100[:, 2]), median(rl100_beliefs[:, 2]))
```

### GPD example

In the second example, you fit a GPD with a trend in the log scale, using the same centered year as the covariate.
The synthetic storm record has 12 storms a year above a threshold of 25.4 mm, and the scale of each storm's excess grows by 0.4% per year.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| output: false
x_storm = repeat(x; inner=12)
peaks_syn = 25.4 .+ rand.(rng, GeneralizedPareto.(0, 20 .* exp.(0.004 .* x_storm), 0.15))
```

`gpfitbayes` takes the peaks and the threshold $u$ and fits a GPD to the excesses.
Its log scale is a straight line in the covariate, where $x_i$ is the year of storm $i$ minus 1985:

$$
y_i - u \sim \text{GPD}\left(\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i), \; \xi\right).
$$

```{julia}
#| solution: false
gp_syn = gpfitbayes(peaks_syn, 25.4; logscalecov=[x_storm], rng=rng, progress=false)
DataFrame(summarystats(gp_syn.estimate))
```

A GPD has no location parameter to trend, so you pass only `logscalecov`.
A GPD return level also needs `rate`, the average number of storms per year above the threshold, which is 12 here.
`gpfit` and `gpfitbayes` treat `rate` as one known number: they do not allow a trend in how often storms exceed the threshold, and their return-level intervals leave out the uncertainty in `rate`.
If you want to model either, write the model in Turing directly.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
rl100_gp = returnlevel(gp_syn, 100; rate=12, logscalecov=[x_report])
println("100-year level in 2026 (mm): ", interval(rl100_gp[:, 2]))
println("Change, 1986 to 2026 (mm): ", interval(rl100_gp[:, 2] .- rl100_gp[:, 1]))
```

With 960 storms in place of 80 annual maxima, the intervals are narrower.

## Your Hobby analysis

Now use the code in the examples to answer the key questions above.
If you fit a GEV, this cell makes a table of annual maxima joined to the covariates:

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| output: false
annmax = combine(groupby(daily, :year), :prcp_mm => maximum => :y)
annmax = sort(innerjoin(annmax, covariates; on=:year), :year)
```

If you fit a GPD, this cell finds the peaks over a threshold and joins each peak's year to the covariates.
The threshold of 25.4 mm and the 72-hour gap between storms are made up to show the code; choose your own and defend them, as in lab 5.
`decluster` keeps the largest day in each storm, and `rate` is the number of peaks per year you kept, which you pass to `returnlevel`.

### Choosing the threshold

A GPD fits the excesses only above a high enough threshold.
Above that threshold, the mean excess should be roughly a straight line in the threshold (@fig-mrl), and the shape $\xi$ and the reparameterized scale $\sigma^* = \sigma_u - \xi u$ should stay roughly constant (@fig-stability).
Both plots use declustered storm peaks above 12.7 mm, so that the days within one storm are not counted twice.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-mrl
#| fig-cap: "Mean residual life of declustered storm peaks at Hobby, with a 95% band."
storm_idx, _ = decluster(DateTime.(daily.date), daily.prcp_mm, 12.7; min_gap_hours=72)
storm_peaks = daily.prcp_mm[storm_idx]
mrl_plot(storm_peaks; lo=12.7, hi=127)
```

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-stability
#| fig-cap: "Parameter stability of the GPD fitted to declustered storm peaks at Hobby, with 95% bands."
stability_plot(storm_peaks; lo_quantile=0.0, hi_quantile=0.97)
```

@tbl-threshold fits a stationary GPD by maximum likelihood at several thresholds and two gaps between storms.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: tbl-threshold
#| tbl-cap: "Number of storm peaks, storms per year, and fitted shape for each threshold and gap."
threshold_table = DataFrame(u_mm=Float64[], gap_hours=Int[], n_peaks=Int[], rate=Float64[], ξ=Float64[])
for u_try in (25.4, 38.1, 50.8, 63.5, 76.2), gap in (48, 72)
    idx, _ = decluster(DateTime.(daily.date), daily.prcp_mm, u_try; min_gap_hours=gap)
    fit = gpfit(daily.prcp_mm[idx], u_try)
    push!(threshold_table, (u_try, gap, length(idx), round(length(idx) / length(keep); digits=2), round(params(fit).β_shape[1]; digits=2)))
end
threshold_table
```

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| output: false
u = 50.8
peak_idx, _ = decluster(DateTime.(daily.date), daily.prcp_mm, u; min_gap_hours=72)
peaks = innerjoin(daily[peak_idx, [:year, :prcp_mm]], covariates; on=:year)
rate = nrow(peaks) / length(keep)
```

Fit the peaks with the table form, such as `gpfitbayes(peaks, :prcp_mm, u; logscalecovid=[:log_CO2], rng=rng, progress=false)`.

### Choosing the covariate

Log CO2 and GMST both rise over the record, so they may carry the same information.
@tbl-cov-cor gives their correlations over the years kept, and @fig-cov-scatter plots GMST against log CO2.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: tbl-cov-cor
#| tbl-cap: "Correlation between the candidate covariates over the years kept."
cov_names = [:log_CO2, :gmst, :nino34]
cov_kept = filter(r -> r.year in keep, covariates)
cov_cor = round.(cor(Matrix(cov_kept[:, cov_names])); digits=2)
cov_cor_table = DataFrame(cov_cor, cov_names)
insertcols!(cov_cor_table, 1, :covariate => string.(cov_names))
```

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-cov-scatter
#| fig-cap: "GMST anomaly against log CO2 in each year kept, colored by year."
fig = Figure(; size=(500, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel="log CO2", ylabel="GMST anomaly (°C)")
sc = scatter!(ax, cov_kept.log_CO2, cov_kept.gmst; color=cov_kept.year, markersize=7)
Colorbar(fig[1, 2], sc; label="year")
fig
```

@tbl-lr compares a trend in the log scale on each covariate with the stationary GPD, fitted by maximum likelihood.
Twice the gain in log likelihood is compared with 3.84, the 95% point of a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: tbl-lr
#| tbl-cap: "Slope of the log scale per unit of each covariate and twice the gain in log likelihood over the stationary GPD."
gp_stat = gpfit(peaks, :prcp_mm, u)
lr_table = DataFrame(covariate=String[], slope=Float64[], twice_ΔLL=Float64[])
for c in cov_names
    fit = gpfit(peaks, :prcp_mm, u; logscalecovid=[c])
    push!(lr_table, (string(c), round(params(fit).β_logscale[2]; digits=3), round(2 * (loglike(fit) - loglike(gp_stat)); digits=2)))
end
lr_table
```

### Is the storm rate changing?

`gpfitbayes` holds the number of storms per year fixed, so check whether it trends.
@fig-storm-rate counts the storm peaks above the threshold in each year kept.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-storm-rate
#| fig-cap: "Storm peaks above the threshold in each year kept at Hobby."
storm_counts = combine(groupby(peaks, :year), nrow => :n)
storm_counts = sort(leftjoin(DataFrame(year=keep), storm_counts; on=:year), :year)
storm_counts.n = coalesce.(storm_counts.n, 0)
@printf("Storms per year: %.2f before 1985, %.2f from 1985; correlation with year %.2f\n",
    mean(storm_counts.n[storm_counts.year .< 1985]), mean(storm_counts.n[storm_counts.year .>= 1985]),
    cor(storm_counts.year, storm_counts.n))

fig = Figure(; size=(700, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{year}", ylabel=L"\text{storms above threshold}")
scatterlines!(ax, storm_counts.year, storm_counts.n; color=colors[1], markersize=5)
fig
```

### Bayesian fit

The log scale is a straight line in log CO2, the shape is constant, and every prior is the flat default:

$$
y_i - u \sim \text{GPD}\left(\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \log \text{CO2}_i), \; \xi\right).
$$

```{julia}
#| solution: false
gp_co2 = gpfitbayes(peaks, :prcp_mm, u; logscalecovid=[:log_CO2], rng=rng, progress=false)
DataFrame(summarystats(gp_co2.estimate))
```

The slope $\beta_1$ is the change in the log scale per unit of log CO2, so a doubling of CO2 multiplies the scale by $2^{\beta_1}$.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
β1 = params(gp_co2).β_logscale[:, 2]
@printf("β1: median %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]; P(β1 > 0) = %.2f\n",
    median(β1), quantile(β1, 0.025), quantile(β1, 0.975), mean(β1 .> 0))
println("Change in scale per doubling of CO2 (%): ", interval(100 .* (2 .^ β1 .- 1)))
```

### Return levels

Each return level needs a CO2 value for its year.
1986 comes from the record.
2026 is the 2025 value plus about 2.5 ppm, the recent yearly rise at Mauna Loa.
2066 depends on future emissions, so it is given for three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs): SSP1-2.6 (low emissions), SSP2-4.5 (middle) and SSP5-8.5 (high).
Table 5 of @meinshausen_sspgreenhouse:2020 gives the global-mean CO2 of each pathway in 2050 and 2075, and the cell interpolates between them in log CO2, which gives about 470, 550 and 706 ppm in 2066.
These are global means, about a part per million below the Mauna Loa values in the record, a difference too small to matter here.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
interval(v) = round.(quantile(v, [0.025, 0.5, 0.975]))   # 2.5%, 50%, 97.5% of the draws, in mm
co2_1986 = covariates.log_CO2[covariates.year .== 1986][1]
co2_2026 = log(exp(covariates.log_CO2[end]) + 2.5)
ssp_co2 = (low=(469.3, 471.0), middle=(506.9, 575.5), high=(562.8, 801.7))   # ppm in 2050 and 2075: SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5
w_2066 = (2066 - 2050) / (2075 - 2050)
co2_2066 = map(c -> (1 - w_2066) * log(c[1]) + w_2066 * log(c[2]), ssp_co2)
@printf("CO2 in 2066 (ppm): low %.0f, middle %.0f, high %.0f\n", exp(co2_2066.low), exp(co2_2066.middle), exp(co2_2066.high))
co2_report = [co2_1986, co2_2026, co2_2066.low, co2_2066.middle, co2_2066.high]

rl10_gp = returnlevel(gp_co2, 10; rate=rate, logscalecov=[co2_report])
rl100_gp = returnlevel(gp_co2, 100; rate=rate, logscalecov=[co2_report])

for (T, rl) in ((10, rl10_gp), (100, rl100_gp))
    println("$T-year level in 2026 (mm): ", interval(rl[:, 2]))
    println("  change, 1986 to 2026 (mm): ", interval(rl[:, 2] .- rl[:, 1]))
    for (k, name) in enumerate(keys(co2_2066))
        println("  change, 2026 to 2066, $name emissions (mm): ", interval(rl[:, 2 + k] .- rl[:, 2]))
    end
end
@printf("100-year trend, 1986 to 2026: median %.2f mm per year, to compare with 1.93 from Fagnant et al.\n",
    median(rl100_gp[:, 2] .- rl100_gp[:, 1]) / 40)
```

@fig-rl-time plots the 10- and 100-year levels in each year of the record, with the annual maxima for reference.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-rl-time
#| fig-cap: "The 10- and 100-year daily rainfall at Hobby through the record from the GPD fit on log CO2 (posterior median and 95% interval), and the annual maxima."
fig = Figure(; size=(700, 350))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{year}", ylabel=L"\text{daily rainfall (mm)}")
for (k, T) in enumerate([10, 100])
    rl = returnlevel(gp_co2, T; rate=rate, logscalecov=[cov_kept.log_CO2])
    band!(ax, cov_kept.year, quantile.(eachcol(rl), 0.025), quantile.(eachcol(rl), 0.975); color=(colors[k], 0.2))
    lines!(ax, cov_kept.year, median.(eachcol(rl)); color=colors[k], linewidth=2, label="$T-year level")
end
scatter!(ax, annmax.year, annmax.y; color=:black, markersize=5, label="annual maxima")
axislegend(ax; position=:lt)
fig
```

### Sensitivity to the threshold

@tbl-threshold-sensitivity refits the same model at a higher threshold, 63.5 mm (2.5 inches), with the same 72-hour gap, and compares the 100-year levels with the fit at 50.8 mm.
If the threshold is high enough, raising it should change the levels little beyond widening the intervals.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: tbl-threshold-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "The 100-year level in 2026 and its changes, in mm (2.5%, 50%, 97.5%), at two thresholds; the 2066 change uses the middle emissions scenario."
sensitivity = DataFrame(u_mm=Float64[], n_peaks=Int[], rl100_2026=String[], change_1986_2026=String[], change_2026_2066=String[])
for u_try in (50.8, 63.5)
    idx, _ = decluster(DateTime.(daily.date), daily.prcp_mm, u_try; min_gap_hours=72)
    peaks_try = innerjoin(daily[idx, [:year, :prcp_mm]], covariates; on=:year)
    fit = gpfitbayes(peaks_try, :prcp_mm, u_try; logscalecovid=[:log_CO2], rng=rng, progress=false)
    rl = returnlevel(fit, 100; rate=nrow(peaks_try) / length(keep), logscalecov=[co2_report])
    push!(sensitivity, (u_try, nrow(peaks_try), string(interval(rl[:, 2])),
        string(interval(rl[:, 2] .- rl[:, 1])), string(interval(rl[:, 4] .- rl[:, 2]))))
end
sensitivity
```

## Key questions

All numbers are posterior medians with 95% intervals from the GPD fit on log CO2 above.

**1. What is your best estimate for the 10- and 100-year return levels in 2026?**

The 10-year daily rainfall in 2026 is about 217 mm (8.5 inches), and the 100-year daily rainfall is about 394 mm (15.5 inches).
For scale, the wettest day in the Hobby record is 307 mm, on August 26, 2017, during Hurricane Harvey.

**2. How uncertain are these estimates?**

The 95% interval is 172 to 291 mm for the 10-year level and 274 to 648 mm for the 100-year level.
The 100-year interval is wide because that level is rarer than almost anything in 80 years of data.
These intervals cover only the uncertainty in the model's parameters.
They leave out the uncertainty in the storm rate, which is held fixed at about 4 storms a year; my choice of threshold, declustering gap, covariate and straight-line form; and the chance that days are missing for reasons tied to the rain, such as a gauge failing in a big storm.
The true uncertainty is wider.

**3. How have these return levels changed over the past 40 years?**

From 1986 to 2026, the 10-year level rose by about 20 mm (−23 to +78) and the 100-year level by about 41 mm (−52 to +174), or about 1.0 mm per year (−1.3 to +4.3).
About 80% of the posterior draws of the CO2 slope are positive, so the record leans toward an increase, but both intervals include zero, so no change cannot be ruled out.
@fagnant_spatiotemporal:2020 report 1.93 mm per year (1.50 to 2.35) for the 100-year level at Hobby.
My median is about half of theirs and my interval is much wider, but their value lies inside my interval, so the results do not conflict.
They pooled more than 600 gauges; one gauge cannot pin the trend down as tightly.

**4. How will these return levels change over the next 40 years, and what assumptions do you make in projecting these?**

The change from 2026 to 2066 depends on future CO2:

| Scenario | CO2 in 2066 | 10-year change (mm) | 100-year change (mm) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| SSP1-2.6 (low) | 470 ppm | +9 (−9 to +44) | +19 (−19 to +98) |
| SSP2-4.5 (middle) | 550 ppm | +26 (−23 to +140) | +55 (−50 to +311) |
| SSP5-8.5 (high) | 706 ppm | +57 (−42 to +371) | +120 (−91 to +816) |

Every interval includes zero.
The projection assumes that the log scale of storm size stays a straight line in log CO2 beyond the range of the data, that the number of storms above the threshold stays at about 4 a year, and that CO2 follows the SSP pathways of @meinshausen_sspgreenhouse:2020, interpolated to 2066.
The intervals widen with emissions because higher CO2 extrapolates further past the record.

## Key decisions

**1. GEV or GPD?**

I fit a GPD to peaks over a threshold, because it uses 317 storms instead of 80 annual maxima.
I kept the years with at least 350 valid days, from 1940 to 2025, which leaves 80 years.
I declustered with a 72-hour gap, so rain days less than three days apart count as one storm and only its largest day is kept; gaps of 48 and 120 hours change the number of storms by less than 3%.
I chose a threshold of 50.8 mm (2 inches) because the mean residual life plot is roughly straight and the shape parameter is roughly stable from about 50 to 65 mm (@fig-mrl, @fig-stability, @tbl-threshold), while still leaving about 4 storms a year.
Refitting at 63.5 mm gives nearly the same 2026 100-year level (@tbl-threshold-sensitivity).

**2. Stationary or nonstationary?**

I fit a nonstationary model because the question is whether rainfall is changing, and warmer air holds about 7% more water vapor per °C.
None of the covariates gives a significant improvement over the stationary model in a likelihood-ratio test (@tbl-lr), so I use the model to measure the trend and its uncertainty rather than to claim one.
I let the log scale depend on log CO2.
Log CO2 and GMST are correlated at 0.96 (@tbl-cov-cor), so I used only one; I chose log CO2 because it is the physical driver and the SSP scenarios give its value in 2066.
Niño 3.4 has no long-term trend and explained almost nothing.
The number of storms per year shows no trend (correlation with year 0.03, @fig-storm-rate), so I held the rate fixed and let only storm size change.

**3. How did you estimate your uncertainty?**

I used a Bayesian fit with `gpfitbayes` and the default flat priors on every coefficient, so the result reflects the Hobby record alone.
The chains converged, with `rhat` near 1 and `ess_bulk` in the thousands.
The intervals are the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the posterior draws of each return level.
